q: In thermodynamics, a spontaneous process is one that:
o: Takes place on its own, without continuous help from outside
Takes place only when energy is supplied continuously
Never reaches a state of equilibrium
x: A spontaneous process proceeds by itself once conditions allow. Spontaneity says nothing about speed: some spontaneous changes are very slow.

q: Which process does NOT take place spontaneously?
o: A gas spreading out to fill an empty container
Heat flowing by itself from a cold body to a hot body
Ice melting in a warm room
x: Heat flows naturally from hot to cold; the reverse needs outside work, as in a refrigerator. The other changes happen on their own.

q: A candle does not burn until it is lit, but once lit it keeps burning by itself. Which statement is correct?
o: Burning is non-spontaneous because the candle had to be lit
Burning is spontaneous; lighting only supplies the energy needed to start it
Burning is endothermic, so it needs the match all the time
Burning is spontaneous only while the match is held to it
x: Some spontaneous reactions need initiation. The match supplies the activation energy; after that, the reaction continues on its own.

q: A spontaneous process left to itself is:
o: Reversible at every stage without outside help
Unidirectional, moving towards a state of equilibrium
Always accompanied by a decrease in volume
x: Spontaneous processes go in one natural direction until equilibrium is reached; they do not reverse by themselves.

q: Which statement about the laws of thermodynamics is correct?
o: They are based on experience and do not depend on any theory of atomic structure
They were derived from the structure of the atom
They apply only to chemical reactions, not to physical changes
They can predict the time a reaction takes
x: The laws of thermodynamics summarise experience with bulk matter. They hold whatever theory of atoms is used, but say nothing about reaction time.

q: Water in an open dish slowly evaporates at room temperature. This process is:
x: Evaporation happens by itself, yet it takes in heat (it is endothermic). So a negative ΔH is not essential for a change to be spontaneous.

q: Which of the following is a spontaneous chemical reaction?
o: Rusting of iron in moist air
Decomposition of water into H₂ and O₂ at room temperature
Conversion of CO₂ and H₂O into glucose in the dark
x: Iron rusts by itself, though slowly. Splitting water or NaCl needs electrical energy, and photosynthesis needs light energy.

q: On an enthalpy level diagram for an exothermic reaction, the products are shown:
o: At the same level as the reactants
x: In an exothermic reaction heat is given out, so the products have less enthalpy than the reactants and ΔH is negative.

q: When dilute NaOH is added to dilute HCl, the temperature of the mixture rises from 25 °C to 31 °C. The reaction is:
x: Heat released by the reaction warms the solution, so the reaction is exothermic and ΔH is negative.

q: Which of these equations describes a change that takes in heat from its surroundings?
x: Splitting water into its elements is the reverse of the strongly exothermic burning of hydrogen, so it absorbs heat. Combustion and neutralisation give out heat.

q: Bond energies (kJ mol⁻¹): H–H 436, Cl–Cl 242, H–Cl 431. What is ΔH for H₂(g) + Cl₂(g) → 2HCl(g)?
x: Bonds broken: 436 + 242 = 678 kJ; bonds formed: 2 × 431 = 862 kJ. ΔH = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ, so the reaction is exothermic.

q: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), ΔH = +178 kJ. How much heat is needed to decompose 50 g of CaCO₃? (Ca = 40, C = 12, O = 16)
x: Molar mass of CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹, so 50 g = 0.5 mol. Heat = 0.5 × 178 = 89 kJ absorbed.

q: Which of these changes is exothermic?
x: A chlorine atom releases energy when it gains an electron (electron affinity). Ionisation, melting and sublimation all absorb energy.

q: Aluminium powder reacts with iron(III) oxide (the thermite reaction) to give so much heat that the iron formed is molten. This reaction is:
o: Endothermic, but heat is released from the iron
x: The thermite reaction gives out enough heat to melt iron, which is why it is used for welding rails. Heat given out means ΔH is negative.

q: Which pair of changes are BOTH endothermic?
o: Evaporation of ethanol and sublimation of iodine
Combustion of ethanol and freezing of water
Condensation of steam and melting of ice
Neutralisation of an acid and respiration of glucose
x: Evaporation and sublimation separate particles against their attractions, so both absorb heat. Combustion, freezing, condensation, neutralisation and respiration release heat.

q: A beaker of water boiling on a burner, with no lid, is an example of:
x: Both energy (heat) and matter (steam) pass across the boundary of an open beaker, so it is an open system.

q: A sealed glass flask containing a gas is heated from outside. The gas in the flask is an example of:
x: A closed system can exchange energy, here heat through the glass, but not matter, because the flask is sealed.

q: Which pair of properties are BOTH state functions?
x: Pressure, temperature, internal energy and enthalpy depend only on the state of the system. Heat and work depend on the path.

q: The heat capacity of an object is the amount of heat needed to raise the temperature of:
o: 1 g of the object by 1 K
1 mol of the object by 1 K
The object to its boiling point
x: Heat capacity refers to the whole object (J K⁻¹). Per gram it is the specific heat capacity, and per mole the molar heat capacity.

q: 2.1 kJ of heat is supplied to 100 g of water. By how much does its temperature rise? (specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹)
x: ΔT = q/(m c) = 2100/(100 × 4.2) = 5 K. Forgetting to change kJ into J would give a far too small rise.

q: For a reaction at constant pressure, ΔH = ΔE + PΔV. ΔH is greater than ΔE when:
o: The volume of the system decreases
No gases take part in the reaction
The reaction is carried out at constant volume
Gas is produced, so the volume of the system increases
x: If the volume increases, PΔV is positive, so ΔH = ΔE + PΔV is larger than ΔE, e.g. CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. With no change in volume the two are equal.

q: A change in which no heat enters or leaves the system, because the system is thermally insulated, is called:
x: Adiabatic means q = 0. Isothermal is constant temperature, isobaric constant pressure and isochoric constant volume.

q: Which statement about the internal energy, E, of a system is correct?
o: It can be measured directly with a thermometer
Its absolute value cannot be measured; only the change, ΔE, can be found
It depends on how the system reached its present state
It is zero for every element at room temperature
x: Internal energy includes all kinetic and potential energies of the particles, so its total cannot be measured. ΔE can be found, and E is a state function.

q: The SI unit of energy, used for internal energy, heat and work, is named after:
x: The joule (J) is named after J. P. Joule, who studied the relation between heat and work. Watt, newton and pascal are units of power, force and pressure.

q: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to:
o: Raise the temperature of 1 kg of water by 1 °C
Raise the temperature of 1 g of water by 1 °C
x: One calorie raises 1 g of water by 1 °C (about 4.184 J). The heat for 1 kg of water would be a kilocalorie.

q: Work and energy are sometimes expressed in dm³ atm. One dm³ atm is equal to about:
x: 1 atm = 101 325 Pa and 1 dm³ = 10⁻³ m³, so 1 dm³ atm = 101.3 Pa m³ = 101.3 J. 8.314 and 0.0821 are values of R.

q: In the older CGS system, energy is measured in ergs. One joule is equal to:
x: 1 J = 1 kg m² s⁻² = 1000 g × 10⁴ cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ g cm² s⁻² = 10⁷ erg.

q: Which set of quantities are ALL measured in joules?
x: Heat, work and internal energy are all forms or amounts of energy, so their unit is the joule. Heat capacity is in J K⁻¹ and pressure in pascals.

q: The unit of molar heat capacity is:
x: Molar heat capacity is energy per mole per kelvin. J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ is the unit of specific heat capacity and J K⁻¹ that of heat capacity.

q: Which of the following is the largest amount of energy? (1 cal = 4.184 J)
x: 1 kJ = 1000 J; 100 cal = 418.4 J; 10⁹ erg = 10⁹/10⁷ = 100 J; so 1 kJ is the largest.

q: Taking w as the work done on the system, the first law of thermodynamics is written as:
x: The change in internal energy equals the heat absorbed plus the work done on the system. With w as work done by the system, it becomes ΔE = q − w.

q: In the convention ΔE = q + w, heat absorbed by the system and work done by the system are taken as:
o: Heat negative, work done by the system positive
Heat positive, work done by the system negative
x: Anything that adds energy to the system is positive. Absorbed heat adds energy; work done by the system removes energy, so it is negative.

q: Heating a gas supplies 300 J to it, while the surroundings also compress it with 100 J of work. By how much does the internal energy of the gas change? (ΔE = q + w)
x: q = +300 J and w = +100 J, so ΔE = 300 + 100 = +400 J. Both heat in and work on the system raise its internal energy.

q: The internal energy of a system falls by 80 J while the system does 30 J of work on the surroundings. What is q? (ΔE = q + w)
x: ΔE = −80 J and w = −30 J (work done by the system). q = ΔE − w = −80 − (−30) = −50 J, so the system gives out 50 J of heat.

q: A machine that does work forever without taking energy from any source (a perpetual motion machine of the first kind) is impossible because it would:
o: Need a catalyst that is used up
Create energy, against the first law of thermodynamics
Have to work at constant volume
Need an activation energy of zero
x: The first law says energy cannot be created; work out without energy in would create energy.

q: An ideal gas expands at constant temperature, so its internal energy does not change. It absorbs 250 J of heat. Which is correct? (ΔE = q + w)
o: The gas does 250 J of work on the surroundings
The gas does 500 J of work on the surroundings
250 J of work is done on the gas
x: ΔE = 0, so w = −q = −250 J. A negative w means 250 J of work is done by the gas: all the heat taken in is used for expansion.

q: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the total energy of the universe:
x: System plus surroundings make up the universe. Energy lost by one is gained by the other, so the total energy stays constant.

q: Nitrogen dioxide can be made from the elements in two steps: forming 2 mol NO absorbs 180 kJ, then oxidising those 2 mol NO to 2 mol NO₂ releases 114 kJ. What is ΔH for N₂ + 2O₂ → 2NO₂ directly?
x: Adding the two steps gives the direct route, so by Hess's law ΔH = +180 + (−114) = +66 kJ.

q: Ethene burns: C₂H₄ + 3O₂ → 2CO₂ + 2H₂O(l). Using enthalpies of formation C₂H₄ +52, CO₂ −394 and H₂O(l) −286 kJ mol⁻¹, find its molar heat of combustion.
x: ΔH = [2(−394) + 2(−286)] − (+52) = −1360 − 52 = −1412 kJ mol⁻¹. Adding the +52 instead of subtracting it gives −1308.

q: For 2X → Y, ΔH = −40 kJ. What is ΔH for 4X → 2Y?
x: Multiplying an equation by 2 doubles its ΔH: 2 × (−40) = −80 kJ. The sign changes only when the equation is reversed.

q: Hess's law of constant heat summation is a consequence of:
o: The first law of thermodynamics (conservation of energy)
x: If two routes between the same states gave different ΔH, energy could be created by going one way and returning the other, which breaks the first law.

q: ΔHf values (kJ mol⁻¹): H₂O₂(l) −188, H₂O(l) −286. What is ΔH for 2H₂O₂(l) → 2H₂O(l) + O₂(g)?
x: ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = 2(−286) − 2(−188) = −572 + 376 = −196 kJ. ΔHf of O₂ is zero.

q: In an energy cycle, X can change into Z directly (ΔH₁), or first into Y (ΔH₂) and then into Z (ΔH₃). According to Hess's law:
x: The enthalpy change from X to Z is the same by either route, so the direct value equals the sum of the steps of the indirect route.

q: Given: C(s) + O₂ → CO₂, ΔH = −394 kJ; H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O(l), ΔH = −286 kJ; C₂H₂ + 2½O₂ → 2CO₂ + H₂O(l), ΔH = −1300 kJ. What is ΔHf of ethyne, C₂H₂?
Anhydrous CuSO₄ dissolves in water with ΔH = −66 kJ mol⁻¹, and CuSO₄·5H₂O dissolves with ΔH = +12 kJ mol⁻¹. What is ΔH for CuSO₄(s) + 5H₂O(l) → CuSO₄·5H₂O(s)?
x: Both salts give the same solution, so ΔH(hydration) = −66 − (+12) = −78 kJ mol⁻¹. This ΔH cannot be measured directly, so Hess's law is used.

q: The enthalpy of a reaction is the heat change when:
o: 1 g of each reactant reacts at constant volume
The reaction reaches equilibrium at constant volume
The moles of reactants shown in the balanced equation react completely at constant pressure
One mole of product is formed from its elements
x: ΔH of reaction refers to the amounts in the balanced equation, at constant pressure. Forming one mole from elements is the special case of enthalpy of formation.

q: The enthalpy of solution of a substance is the enthalpy change when one mole of it:
o: Dissolves in exactly 1 dm³ of water
Is formed from its ions in solution
Dissolves in so much solvent that further dilution causes no heat change
x: Enthalpy of solution is measured at infinite dilution, when adding more solvent gives no further heat change.

q: In the FSc convention, standard enthalpy changes are measured at a pressure of:
x: In the FSc convention, standard conditions are 298 K and 1 atm pressure (101.325 kPa), with solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³.

q: Which equation represents the standard enthalpy of combustion of carbon monoxide?
x: Enthalpy of combustion is for 1 mol of the substance burning completely. The second equation burns 2 mol, and the last two burn carbon, not CO.

q: The standard enthalpy of formation of ammonia corresponds to which reaction?
x: Formation means 1 mol of compound from its elements in their standard states. N₂ + 3H₂ gives 2 mol, and N(g), H(g) atoms are not standard states.

q: 200 cm³ of 0.5 mol dm⁻³ H₂SO₄ is fully neutralised by excess NaOH. Taking ΔH of neutralisation as −57 kJ per mole of water formed, how much heat is released?
x: Moles of H₂SO₄ = 0.2 × 0.5 = 0.1, giving 0.2 mol H⁺ and so 0.2 mol H₂O. Heat = 0.2 × 57 = 11.4 kJ. Forgetting the two H⁺ gives 5.7 kJ.

q: Standard enthalpies of combustion of substances are always:
o: Positive, because oxygen bonds must be broken
Negative, because combustion gives out heat
Positive for elements and negative for compounds
x: Combustion is always exothermic, so ΔH of combustion is negative for every fuel.
